name: PHA (polyhydroxy acid)

lead: Polyhydroxy acids carry several hydroxyl groups and are used in skincare as mild exfoliants and humectants. The two usually named are gluconolactone and lactobionic acid. They are used for smoother, brighter-looking, hydrated skin, including skin that stings easily with acids like glycolic.

Their larger molecular size is said to slow penetration, and their hydroxyl groups bind water and metal ions, adding moisturising and antioxidant behaviour. A summary of small trials reports performance similar to AHAs in some measures with less stinging in some comparisons.

paras: People use PHAs in toners, serums and mild peels as a lower-irritation step in an exfoliation routine, often by those new to acids or with sensitive skin. Results build gradually with regular use.
Described as well tolerated. Regulators say AHAs in general can raise sunburn likelihood, and sun protection is commonly advised on labels.

angle.text: PHAs, mainly gluconolactone and lactobionic acid, are gentler cousins of AHAs used for smoother, brighter skin, including skin that stings easily. Large molecules exfoliate the surface slowly while holding water; small trials report similar results to AHAs with less stinging.

lead: Polyhydroxy acids (PHAs) are a group of organic acids that carry multiple hydroxyl groups and are used in skincare as mild exfoliants, humectants and antioxidants. The two usually named are gluconolactone and lactobionic acid.[1][2] People use them to smooth rough texture, brighten dullness and keep skin hydrated, and they are particularly popular among those whose skin reacts to stronger acids such as glycolic acid.

Gluconolactone is the lactone of gluconic acid, an oxidised derivative of glucose, and lactobionic acid is a disaccharide of gluconic acid and galactose.[2][3] Because their molecules are larger than those of the alpha hydroxy acids (AHAs), manufacturers and some reviewers say they penetrate more slowly and stay nearer the surface, which is the proposed reason for lower stinging.[1]

A summary of the small trial literature reports performance similar to AHAs on some measures with less stinging in some comparisons.[1] Larger independent trials have not been published, and much of the class is described in manufacturer and review material.
infobox: Toners, serums, leave-on and rinse-off products, peels

paras: Gluconolactone is used both as the food additive E575 and in leave-on and rinse-off cosmetics.[1][2] Lactobionic acid, formula C12H22O12, is a sugar acid made of gluconic acid and galactose, formed by oxidising lactose and listed as food additive E399.[3] Its calcium salt is used as a food stabiliser, its potassium salt is added to organ-preservation solutions such as Viaspan and CoStorSol to give osmotic support, and it is used in cosmetics as an antioxidant.[3] A 2012 study of its use in topical emulsions is cited on Wikipedia.[3]

Like AHAs, PHAs are acids that loosen the bonds between cells in the outer skin layer, so that dead cells shed more readily. AHAs such as glycolic and lactic acid are the best-known chemical exfoliants in cosmetics.[4] PHAs differ by carrying several hydroxyl groups, which bind water and metal ions; manufacturers cite this for moisturising and antioxidant behaviour alongside mild exfoliation.[1][3] Their larger size is said to slow penetration, though comparative penetration data are limited.

PHAs appear in cleansers, toners, serums and peel products, often marketed to people with rosacea-prone, eczema-prone or generally sensitive skin, and to those starting acid exfoliation. They are also combined with retinoids or other actives in routines, with proponents saying that the lower irritation allows steadier use. Gluconolactone additionally features in some formulations as a mild preservative-supporting ingredient, according to ingredient summaries.[1]

No class-level clinical trials were found. For gluconolactone specifically, Grokipedia summarises small comparisons with glycolic acid and benzoyl peroxide, including one 150-patient acne trial, reporting fewer side effects with gluconolactone.[1] These summaries have not been independently checked against the original papers.

The Cosmetic Ingredient Review is reported to have found gluconolactone safe at current use levels.[1] For the AHA class, the FDA and CIR have said safety depends on low concentration, pH above 3.5 and safety instructions, with mild irritation, redness and flaking the most common side effects.[4] The FDA has also cautioned that AHAs can raise the likelihood of sunburn, an effect that reverses when use stops; other sources cited on the Wikipedia AHA page suggest glycolic acid may protect against some sun damage.[4] Product labels for exfoliating acids commonly advise daily sunscreen use.

PHA products have been promoted in the cosmetics press and by brands as a gentle alternative to glycolic acid, and the term is as much a marketing category as a chemical one, with brands applying it to products containing gluconolactone, lactobionic acid or related sugar acids.[1] The abbreviation PHA is also used for unrelated topics such as pseudohypoaldosteronism and polyhydroxyalkanoate bioplastics, which are not connected to the skincare ingredients.
